description_full: Newmark Group, Inc. operates as a commercial real estate advisor and service provider in the United States, the United Kingdom, Asia, rest of Europe, and other Americas. The company offers capital markets services consisting of investment sales, including placement and raising of equity; and commercial mortgage brokerage, such as government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) and federal housing administration (FHA) lending, as well as the placement of debt, loan sales, and structured finance on behalf of third parties. It also provides landlord or agency representation leasing; GSEs and FHA multifamily loan servicing, as well as limited loan servicing, special loan servicing, and asset management; management consulting, managed services, and fund accounting for investors; valuation and advisory services; property management and workspace solutions for owners; due diligence, consulting, and other advisory services; commercial real estate technology platform and capabilities; and business rates for property owners. In addition, the company offers tenant representation leasing; occupier solutions comprising project management, transaction management, lease administration, and facilities management, as well as corporate consulting services to real estate and supply chain optimization, workplace strategy, and occupancy strategy areas; workspace solutions for occupiers; and business rates for occupiers. It serves commercial real estate tenants, investors, owners, occupiers, and developers, lenders, small and medium size businesses, multi-national corporations, and institutional owners of real estate. The company was formerly known as Newmark Grubb Knight Frank Capital Group and changed its name to Newmark Group, Inc. in October 2017. Newmark Group, Inc. was founded in 1929 and is based in New York, New York. Newmark Group, Inc. operates as a subsidiary of Cantor Fitzgerald, L.P.

financial_summary: Newmark Group, Inc. is a mid-cap real estate business with a $2.6B market cap on $3.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $143M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.36× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 4.2×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 2.4% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sect: Its 7% operating margin trails the Real Estate median (23%) by 16pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.36x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.9% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-7.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 28% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 42% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 42% and a beta of 1.19, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.34 vs 5y 1.29), so read it loosely.
About $24.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 80% in the 2020 crash and 59% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 34% below its DCF fair value of $16.05, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 44%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $11.39 to $23.06 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Real Estate peers: P/E 13.1 vs 23.9 and EV/EBITDA 10.4 vs 16.2 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 1% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $16.75 on average, 58% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 9.4%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.27).
It converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.36x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 4%.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.4x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.1x net debt to EBITDA ($229.1M of cash against $671.7M of debt), with interest covered 4.2x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.67 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.8% over 3 years and 11.6% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 21%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00 and a backlog worth 4% of annual revenue.
Capex runs only 0.2x depreciation (0.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.1% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.4%, and institutions hold 80%.
It returns 5.8% a year to shareholders (4.9% in buybacks and 2.3% in dividends).
people: With about 10,500 employees, each generates about $314K of revenue, 0.1x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 7.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $14K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (9x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
